what_its_for: Luspatercept-aamt is used to treat anemia (low red blood cell counts) in adults. It is approved for anemia caused by beta-thalassemia (a blood disorder you are born with), myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS, a type of bone marrow disease), or myelodysplastic syndrome or myeloproliferative neoplasm-associated myelofibrosis (MDS/MPN with ring sideroblasts). It works by helping your body make more mature red blood cells so you need fewer blood transfusions.
how_to_take: This medicine is given as a shot (injection) under your skin (subcutaneous injection), usually in your upper arm, thigh, or belly area. A doctor, nurse, or other trained healthcare provider will give you this injection in a clinic or hospital setting. Do NOT try to inject it yourself at home unless your healthcare team has specifically trained you to do so. Each injection is given once every 3 weeks (21 days).
dosing: Your doctor will decide the right dose for you based on your weight and your condition. The usual starting dose is 1 mg per kilogram of your body weight, given once every 3 weeks. Your doctor may increase your dose over time (up to 1.75 mg/kg) if your body needs a higher amount to raise your red blood cell levels. Never change your dose on your own — always follow your doctor's instructions.
missed_dose: If you miss or forget your scheduled injection appointment, call your doctor or clinic right away to reschedule as soon as possible. After you get the missed dose, your next dose should be scheduled 3 weeks (21 days) after that make-up injection. Try to keep all of your scheduled appointments so your treatment stays on track.
storage: Luspatercept-aamt is stored and handled by healthcare professionals in a medical setting. If you are ever given vials to store at home, keep them in the refrigerator at 36°F to 46°F (2°C to 8°C). Do NOT freeze the medicine. Keep it in the original box to protect it from light. Once the medicine is mixed (reconstituted), it should be used right away or stored in the refrigerator and used within 8 hours. Keep all medicines out of the reach of children and pets.
what_to_avoid: Tell your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding before starting this medicine — it can harm an unborn baby. Women who can become pregnant must use effective birth control during treatment and for at least 3 months after the last dose. Men with female partners who can become pregnant should also use birth control during treatment and for 3 months after the last dose. Avoid activities that could increase your risk of falls or injury if you feel dizzy or faint, since this medicine can cause dizziness. Let all your doctors know about every medicine, vitamin, or supplement you take.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you experience any of the following: sudden severe headache, dizziness, confusion, or vision changes (these could be signs of a dangerous rise in blood pressure); chest pain, shortness of breath, pain or swelling in your leg (possible blood clot or stroke warning signs); signs of a serious allergic reaction such as hives, swelling of your face or throat, trouble breathing; unusual or severe pain at the injection site; feeling very tired, weak, or short of breath (signs your anemia may not be improving). Also call your doctor if you are pregnant or think you might be pregnant during treatment.
when_it_works: Luspatercept-aamt does not work overnight. Most patients start to see improvements in their red blood cell counts or a reduction in the need for blood transfusions after a few weeks of treatment. Some patients may need up to 24 weeks (about 6 months) or longer to see the full benefit. Your doctor will check your blood counts regularly to see how well the medicine is working for you. If there is no improvement after a certain period of time, your doctor may decide to stop the treatment.
special_populations: Pregnancy and breastfeeding: This medicine can cause serious harm to an unborn baby. Do not use it if you are pregnant. Stop breastfeeding during treatment and for 3 months after the last dose because it is not known if the medicine passes into breast milk. Older adults (age 65 and over): This medicine can be used in older adults, but your doctor will monitor you carefully for side effects such as high blood pressure and fatigue. Kidney or liver problems: Tell your doctor if you have kidney or liver disease, as your doctor may need to monitor you more closely. Children: This medicine has not been approved for use in children under 18 years of age.
